reader.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Brown at Moorhead, Minnesota
bases: A mob of several hundred went to the county jail at Moorhead to seize and lynch a prisoner accused of killing a policeman, but he had been removed and no one was hurt (A3, A4, A6).
A mob of 400 to 500 men sought to lynch Brown for the killing of Policeman Poull, an extralegal act under the pretext of justice, but the sheriff had removed him and no one was killed (A3, A6, A10).

A Moorhead special to the St. Paul Globe and a separate wire report carried in the Great Falls Tribune agree on a mob of several hundred at the jail, the sheriff's removal of the prisoner and the committee search (A3, A6), and a third text agrees on the crowd and the removal (A7).

summary.text: The attempted lynching of Thomas Brown took place shortly after midnight on October 18-19, 1888, when a mob of several hundred men went to the county jail at Moorhead, Minnesota, to lynch a prisoner accused of killing a policeman.
Sheriff Jensen had already removed the wounded prisoner, and the crowd dispersed after a committee searched the jail.
Papers across the Midwest and Northwest carried the story, and one wire report commended the sheriff.

According to the St. Paul Globe's Moorhead correspondent, Fargo police suspected a man known as Murphy of a robbery at the Manitoba house in Fargo and followed him to a dance at Erickson's hall in Moorhead on the evening of October 17.
When officers tried to arrest him, he drew a revolver, marched them downstairs, and shot Moorhead officer Pete Poull through the heart at about 12:30 a.m. on October 18.
Officer John Thompson returned fire and brought him down with several wounds, and the prisoner was carried to the jail in critical condition.
Other reports named the accused Thomas Brown and called him a "professional crook" whom police suspected of burglaries in Fargo.
One account said that during the day there had been "strong talk of lynching Brown," and that such a fate "would surprise no one."
Expecting a mob, Sheriff Jensen and a deputy drove the prisoner out of town by carriage on Thursday evening and kept him in the country overnight.
Shortly after midnight a crowd the Globe put at 400 and a wire report at 500 came to the jail, carrying railroad iron, jack screws and sledge hammers to break through the walls.
The wire said the mob had been "organized at Fargo," called its members "maddened by liquor," and said many in the crowd were only spectators.
A deputy at the jail door proposed that the crowd choose a committee to search the building.
The committee did not find the prisoner, and the mob dispersed.

The next morning the sheriff boarded a train at Tenney, a flag station east of Moorhead, and took the prisoner to the Hennepin county jail in Minneapolis to be held until his arraignment before Judge Mills.
Poull was buried on October 20 at a largely attended funeral.
On November 2 Fargo police arrested Ben Bennett, alias James Kelley, on suspicion of being Brown's partner.

By December 18 Brown, "whose life has twice been threatened by Moorhead mobs," was held in the Otter Tail county jail at Fergus Falls, where he told a reporter he expected to hang unless his trial was moved out of Clay County.
No report of the outcome of his trial appears in the coverage, and none of the mob was reported arrested.

The St. Paul Globe covered the case most fully, with Moorhead specials under headlines such as "A MURDERER'S DANGER" and "SAFE FROM THE MOB" that called the prisoner the murderer of Poull before any trial.
A wire version ran in the Great Falls Tribune on October 24 and in the Bismarck Weekly Tribune two days later, under the headline "A Mob of Moorhead Men Attempt to Form a Lynching Party."
That version both blamed the "desperate men" for drinking and closed with the line that "the sheriff's action is commended."
A second text, printed in the New Ulm Weekly Review and The Sun, gave the prisoner's criminal reputation and said a lynching would surprise no one.
By October 27 the story had shrunk to a single sentence in a Michigan weekly's regional news column, which placed the jail at Fargo, Dakota Territory.
No paper gave the race of the accused or of the mob.

The Globe's Moorhead specials put the jail at Moorhead, where the case was later to be tried, while the Michigan brief placed it at Fargo, apparently compressing the wire's statement that the mob was "organized at Fargo."
Papers also spelled the policeman's name as Poull, Paull, Poole and Toole, and called the accused either Murphy or Thomas Brown.

accounts.label: Moorhead special to the St. Paul Globe
accounts.gist: A mob of 400 went to the county jail shortly after midnight to lynch Murphy; Sheriff Jensen had taken him away in a hack, and a committee searched the jail without finding him.

accounts.label: Wire report (Great Falls Tribune, Bismarck Tribune)
accounts.gist: A mob of 500 'organized at Fargo' with railroad iron, jack screws and sledge hammers would have hanged the prisoner had the sheriff not removed him; a deputy proposed a committee search, after which the mob dispersed.

accounts.label: Fargo-centered report (New Ulm Review, The Sun)
accounts.gist: After a day of 'strong talk of lynching', a crowd of several hundred carried a railroad tie to the jail but found the prisoner gone.

framing.detail: The St. Paul Globe headlined 'A MURDERER'S DANGER' and 'THE JAIL IS SEARCHED' and treated Murphy's guilt as settled while praising the 'plucky' officer.
The wire called the mob 'desperate men, maddened by liquor' and commended the sheriff, while another report said a lynching 'would surprise no one'.
Distant papers ran the mob as a one-sentence brief among regional news items.
